stem: Under the Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM) Step 4.3, what action must evaluators take if the randomly selected sample set reveals types of web content or evaluation outcomes that were not present in the structured sample set?

options.text: Return to Step 3 and expand the sample set to include the newly identified types of content and findings.
Exclude the unexpected findings from the final conformance report because they fell outside the structured evaluation plan.
Immediately issue a failed conformance evaluation report without auditing the remainder of the random sample.
Discard the structured sample set and replace the entire evaluation with an exclusively randomized audit.

explanation: According to WCAG-EM Step 4.3 (Compare structured and random sample sets), if the randomly selected sample set shows new types of content or new evaluation findings, it indicates that the structured sample set was not sufficiently representative. Evaluators must return to Step 3 (Select a representative sample set) to select additional samples reflecting the newly identified types of content and findings.

distractorNotes.b: Randomly identified defects cannot be discarded; discovering them proves the structured sample was incomplete.
distractorNotes.c: A finding does not terminate the audit immediately; the methodology directs the evaluator to adjust the sample representation before concluding.
distractorNotes.d: The structured sample is maintained and augmented; it is not discarded in favor of purely random testing.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM §4.4.3 Step 4.3 specifies returning to Step 3 to expand the representative sample when random samples surface unrepresented content.

stem: An auditor is testing a dynamic single-page web application with NVDA. When an AJAX call updates a container with aria-live="polite", under what condition will NVDA fail to announce the update while the auditor remains on the page?

options.text: When the live region container has the aria-atomic attribute explicitly set to true on the parent element
When the container element itself was dynamically injected into the DOM at the exact same moment as its text
When the auditor is currently navigating the application document in Browse Mode rather than Focus Mode
When the container element has an explicit accessible role of status applied to it in the HTML markup

explanation: For screen readers including NVDA to detect dynamic updates, the live region container must already exist in the DOM with aria-live present prior to the content insertion. If both the container and its contents are injected simultaneously, NVDA frequently fails to register the mutation.

distractorNotes.a: Setting aria-atomic="true" causes NVDA to announce the entire container contents rather than suppressing the announcement.
distractorNotes.c: NVDA is designed to monitor and speak live region updates in Browse Mode as well as Focus Mode.
distractorNotes.d: An accessible role of status implies aria-live="polite", which enables announcement rather than preventing it.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.6 specifies live region processing models and dynamic container DOM registration requirements.

distractorNotes.a: Pausing or resuming speech output is triggered by a two-finger single tap, not the two-finger double-tap Magic Tap.
distractorNotes.b: Dismissing an alert or navigating back is performed by a two-finger scrub (a 'Z' gesture), not the Magic Tap.
distractorNotes.c: Continuous reading from the top of the page is initiated by a two-finger swipe upward.

sourceNote: W3C WAI evaluation resources explain standard multi-touch accessibility gestures in mobile screen readers.

stem: When conducting a mobile web accessibility audit on an Android device using Google TalkBack, what gesture activates the currently focused button or control?

options.text: Double-tapping anywhere on the screen
options.hintText: activates the focused item in Google TalkBack

options.text: Long-pressing on the screen with two fingers
options.hintText: opens the TalkBack context menu or starts continuous reading

options.text: Swiping upward vertically with one finger
options.hintText: adjusts reading control settings or moves to previous item based on granularity

options.text: Tapping once directly on the targeted control
options.hintText: selects and speaks the touched item without activating it

explanation: In TalkBack on Android, once an element has accessibility focus, double-tapping anywhere on the screen activates it.

distractorNotes.b: Long-pressing with two fingers opens global TalkBack menus or contextual actions.
distractorNotes.c: Swiping up with one finger moves focus according to the selected reading control granularity.
distractorNotes.d: Single tapping moves accessibility focus to the touched item and announces its label, but does not activate it.

sourceNote: W3C WAI guidance defines basic touch navigation gestures for Android TalkBack accessibility audits.

stem: How does an auditor adjust the reading granularity (such as switching from Default to Headings, Links, or Controls) in modern versions of Google TalkBack on Android?

options.text: By rotating two fingers on the display screen in a continuous dial motion
options.hintText: gesture used to operate the VoiceOver rotor on iOS

options.text: By swiping up then down with one finger, or swiping with three fingers
options.hintText: adjusts reading controls and granularity in modern versions of TalkBack

options.text: By pressing the hardware Volume Up and Power buttons at the same instant
options.hintText: hardware button shortcut for capturing screen images on Android devices

options.text: By performing a rapid double-tap gesture on the glass using two fingers
options.hintText: pauses or resumes media playback in mobile screen reader environments

explanation: In modern TalkBack, users cycle through reading controls (Headings, Controls, Links, Characters, Lines) by swiping up then down (or down then up) with one finger, or by swiping left or right with three fingers.

distractorNotes.a: Rotating two fingers is the VoiceOver Rotor gesture on iOS, not Android TalkBack.
distractorNotes.c: Volume Up and Power triggers hardware screenshots or system power menus.
distractorNotes.d: Double-tapping with two fingers pauses or resumes speech or handles phone calls.

sourceNote: W3C WAI testing guidance documents Android TalkBack reading controls and navigation gestures.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Target Size (Minimum), Level AA), what is the minimum required dimensions for pointer targets, unless an exception such as spacing offset or inline text applies?

options.text: 44 by 44 CSS pixels
48 by 48 CSS pixels
24 by 24 CSS pixels
32 by 32 CSS pixels

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires pointer targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or to have sufficient spacing offset. 44 by 44 CSS pixels is the Level AAA threshold under SC 2.5.5.

distractorNotes.a: 44 by 44 CSS pixels is the Level AAA requirement defined under SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced).
distractorNotes.b: 48 by 48 CSS pixels is Google Material Design recommendation, not the WCAG 2.2 Level AA normative requirement.
distractorNotes.d: 32 by 32 CSS pixels is not a normative threshold in WCAG specifications.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 specifies the 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum target size threshold for Level AA conformance.

stem: When evaluating a mobile web application for WCAG 2.1/2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.4 (Orientation, Level AA), which of the following implementations constitutes an accessibility violation?

options.text: A digital piano keyboard app that restricts display to landscape orientation because essential musical keys cannot physically fit in portrait
A check deposit feature that temporarily displays a viewfinder in landscape mode to match the physical aspect ratio of paper checks
A virtual reality 360-degree video simulation that locks display orientation because multi-axis sensor tracking is essential to the experience
An e-commerce checkout page that forces portrait orientation via CSS or JavaScript because the design team preferred vertical layout

explanation: Under SC 1.3.4, content must not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation unless a specific orientation is essential (such as a piano keyboard or bank check). Restricting orientation merely for design preference is a failure.

distractorNotes.a: A piano keyboard application qualifies under the essential exception because piano keys require horizontal layout.
distractorNotes.b: Check deposit viewfinders qualify under the essential exception due to physical aspect ratios of financial documents.
distractorNotes.c: Virtual reality simulations where multi-axis rotational tracking is essential qualify under the essential exception of SC 1.3.4.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.4 requires that web content does not restrict operation to a single display orientation unless essential.

stem: When testing a webpage for conformance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.4 (Resize Text, Level AA), what specific technical condition must be verified when text is resized up to 200 percent?

options.text: Text can be resized up to 200 percent without assistive technology without loss of content or functionality
The layout maintains an identical desktop presentation without wrapping or reflow of page components
Both text and raster graphics must scale by 200 percent simultaneously without bitmap interpolation blur
The webpage must automatically convert all visual text elements into synthetic spoken speech audio

explanation: Under SC 1.4.4, text must be able to be resized without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality (such as text overlapping, clipping, or truncated buttons).

distractorNotes.b: Text reflow, wrapping, and layout shifts are expected and permissible when text size increases.
distractorNotes.c: SC 1.4.4 specifically applies to text, not to raster images or photographic graphics.
distractorNotes.d: Converting text into speech audio is a function of screen readers, not a requirement of SC 1.4.4.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 requires text to be resizable up to 200 percent without assistive technology.

stem: When testing desktop web content for WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow, Level AA), what viewport width and browser zoom setting corresponds to the normative test benchmark?

options.text: 200 percent zoom configured at a 1024 CSS pixels viewport width on standard desktop monitors
400 percent zoom at a 1280 CSS pixels desktop viewport width, equivalent to 320 CSS pixels
150 percent zoom evaluated across a 1920 CSS pixels widescreen high-definition desktop display
500 percent zoom rendered within an 800 CSS pixels legacy desktop browser application window

explanation: SC 1.4.10 requires content to reflow without requiring two-dimensional scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels, which evaluators test on desktop by setting the browser width to 1280 CSS pixels and zooming to 400 percent.

distractorNotes.a: 200 percent zoom at 1024px yields 512 CSS pixels, which is wider than the required 320 CSS pixel threshold.
distractorNotes.c: 150 percent zoom at 1920px tests a 1280px equivalent viewport, which does not evaluate reflow boundaries.
distractorNotes.d: 500 percent zoom exceeds the normative 400 percent (320 CSS pixel) requirement of SC 1.4.10.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 specifies reflow testing at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels (400% zoom at 1280px).

stem: During an audit at 400 percent zoom (320 CSS pixels equivalent width), an evaluator observes horizontal scrolling. Which of the following components is explicitly exempt from the single-direction scrolling mandate of SC 1.4.10?

options.text: Main site navigation menus that expand into nested accordion sub-menu hierarchies
A multi-step checkout form layout containing credit card and customer billing inputs
A complex data table where columns cannot reflow without losing tabular relationships
Standard editorial article paragraphs containing extended narrative text sentences

explanation: SC 1.4.10 provides an exception for content where two-dimensional layout is essential to usage or meaning, such as complex data tables, maps, diagrams, video, games, and presentation slides.

distractorNotes.a: Navigation menus must adapt into responsive patterns without requiring horizontal page scrolling.
distractorNotes.b: Form fields and checkout workflows must reflow vertically without horizontal overflow.
distractorNotes.d: Article paragraphs must wrap lines naturally and must not require horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS pixels.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 explicitly exempts content requiring two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning such as data tables.

stem: What are the minimum contrast ratios required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast (Minimum), Level AA) for regular body text and large-scale text, respectively?

options.text: 3:1 for regular text and 1.5:1 for large text
7:1 for regular text and 4.5:1 for large text
5:1 for regular text and 3:1 for large text
4.5:1 for regular text and 3:1 for large text

explanation: Under SC 1.4.3 (Level AA), regular text requires at least a 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background, while large-scale text (at least 18pt / 24px or 14pt bold / ~18.66px bold) requires at least 3:1.

distractorNotes.a: 3:1 and 1.5:1 fall below the required Level AA standard for readability.
distractorNotes.b: 7:1 for regular text and 4.5:1 for large text are the Level AAA thresholds defined under SC 1.4.6.
distractorNotes.c: 5:1 is not a standard WCAG contrast threshold.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 defines the 4.5:1 and 3:1 contrast ratios for regular and large text at Level AA.

stem: When evaluating a web form for WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast, Level AA), what visual element must maintain at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against adjacent colors?

options.text: Visual boundaries and state indicators (such as focused or active borders) of user interface components
Decorative background gradient patterns and visual styling placed behind promotional hero banners
Corporate brand logos, organization logotypes, and official company visual identity emblems
Inactive and disabled interactive form controls that end users cannot manipulate or select

explanation: SC 1.4.11 requires a 3:1 contrast ratio for user interface components (visual information required to identify components and states) and graphical objects. Disabled controls, logos, and purely decorative graphics are exempt.

distractorNotes.b: Purely decorative visuals and background patterns are explicitly exempt from SC 1.4.11.
distractorNotes.c: Logos and brand text within images are explicitly exempt from non-text contrast requirements.
distractorNotes.d: Inactive and disabled user interface controls are explicitly exempt from contrast requirements.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires 3:1 contrast for user interface component boundaries and graphical objects.

stem: When using a bookmarklet to test WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.12 (Text Spacing, Level AA), which set of CSS style metrics represents the exact normative thresholds that must be supported without loss of content?

options.text: Line height of 2.0 times font size, paragraph spacing of 3.0 times font size, letter spacing of 0.25 times font size, and word spacing of 0.5 times font size
Line height of 1.5 times font size, spacing below paragraphs of 2.0 times font size, letter spacing of 0.12 times font size, and word spacing of 0.16 times font size
Line height of 1.2 times font size, paragraph spacing of 1.5 times font size, letter spacing of 0.05 times font size, and word spacing of 0.10 times font size
Line height of 1.75 times font size, paragraph spacing of 2.5 times font size, letter spacing of 0.20 times font size, and word spacing of 0.30 times font size

explanation: SC 1.4.12 requires that content can adapt without loss of content or functionality to: line height to at least 1.5 times font size; paragraph spacing to at least 2 times font size; letter spacing to at least 0.12 times font size; and word spacing to at least 0.16 times font size.

distractorNotes.a: These metrics exceed the normative metrics established in SC 1.4.12.
distractorNotes.c: These values fall below the required testing thresholds mandated by the criterion.
distractorNotes.d: These arbitrary figures do not reflect the specific four metrics defined in WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 specifies exact spacing metrics: line height 1.5, paragraph 2.0, letter 0.12, word 0.16.

stem: When testing a web application in Windows Contrast Mode (High Contrast Mode), what common CSS design pattern frequently results in a complete loss of visual icons or indicators?

options.text: Providing semantic HTML heading elements structured with clear and descriptive text content
Using inline SVG vector graphics styled with CSS fill properties set to currentColor values
Using CSS background-image icons without corresponding text or high-contrast fallback styling
Using native HTML button elements containing plain visible text labels and standard borders

explanation: In Windows Contrast Mode, the operating system overrides author CSS and strips out CSS background-image properties by default. If icons or indicators are rendered exclusively as CSS background images without high contrast media queries or native HTML/SVG elements, they become completely invisible.

distractorNotes.a: Semantic HTML headings are rendered using system high-contrast colors and remain fully readable.
distractorNotes.b: SVG icons styled with currentColor adapt to the active system text color and remain visible in High Contrast Mode.
distractorNotes.d: Native HTML buttons are rendered with system high-contrast button styling and text colors.

sourceNote: W3C WAI guidance explains how high-contrast operating system modes handle CSS background images and colors.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus, Level AA), which three criteria must additional content (such as a custom tooltip) satisfy when it appears upon pointer hover or keyboard focus?

options.text: Scalable, Animated, and High-Contrast
Responsive, Accessible, and Machine-readable
Modeless, Draggable, and Self-closing
Dismissible, Hoverable, and Persistent

explanation: SC 1.4.13 requires that content appearing on hover or focus must be: Dismissible (can be dismissed without moving pointer or keyboard focus, e.g. pressing Escape), Hoverable (pointer can move over the new content without it disappearing), and Persistent (remains visible until hover/focus is removed or dismissed).

distractorNotes.a: Scalable and animated are general design characteristics rather than the three normative requirements of SC 1.4.13.
distractorNotes.b: Responsive and machine-readable are general technical virtues, not the specific hover/focus rules.
distractorNotes.c: Modeless, draggable, and self-closing describe modal dialog traits rather than tooltip hover criteria.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 specifies that content on hover or focus must be dismissible, hoverable, and persistent.

stem: An evaluator tests a button with speech recognition software (such as Dragon NaturallySpeaking). The button visibly displays the text "Search", but its HTML markup is `<button aria-label="Find products">Search</button>`. What accessibility failure occurs when a user says "Click Search"?

options.text: The command fails under SC 2.5.3 (Label in Name) because the programmatic accessible name does not include the visible text string
The command fails under SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard) because speech software operates exclusively through keyboard emulation drivers
The command succeeds under SC 2.5.3 because speech recognition software ignores aria-label attributes in favor of text nodes
The command fails under SC 1.3.1 because native HTML button elements are prohibited from containing plain text DOM child nodes

explanation: Under SC 2.5.3 (Label in Name, Level A), for components with labels that include text, the accessible name must contain the text presented visually. Because aria-label="Find products" completely overrides "Search", the accessible name is "Find products", causing voice commands targeting "Search" to fail.

distractorNotes.b: Speech software interacts directly with the accessibility tree; it does not fail SC 2.1.1.
distractorNotes.c: Speech engines rely directly on the accessible name computed from ARIA attributes; they do not ignore aria-label.
distractorNotes.d: HTML button elements are designed to contain text nodes; doing so is completely valid HTML.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3 requires the accessible name of an interactive component to contain its visible text label.

stem: When tabbing through a webpage with a sticky bottom cookie banner, keyboard focus lands on an interactive link that is completely hidden underneath the banner. Which WCAG 2.2 success criterion is directly violated?

options.text: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard
options.hintText: requires functionality to be operable through a keyboard interface without specific timings

options.text: SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured
options.hintText: requires that focused components are not entirely hidden due to author-created content

options.text: SC 2.4.3 Focus Order
options.hintText: requires focusable components to receive focus in an order preserving meaning and operability

options.text: SC 3.2.1 On Focus
options.hintText: requires that receiving focus does not initiate an automatic change of context

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA) requires that when an item receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden due to author-created content (such as sticky banners or floating headers).

distractorNotes.a: The element can still receive keyboard focus, so basic keyboard operability under SC 2.1.1 is not the specific violated criterion.
distractorNotes.c: Focus order may follow DOM sequence, but obscuring the visual focused item violates focus visibility and unobscured criteria.
distractorNotes.d: SC 3.2.1 applies to unexpected context changes triggered upon receiving focus, not physical visual obstruction.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 requires that when an item receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden by author-created content.

stem: An auditor evaluates an embedded calendar widget. Pressing Tab moves keyboard focus into the calendar, but subsequent Tab and Shift + Tab presses remain stuck inside the widget, and pressing Escape does not exit. What makes this an unambiguous failure of SC 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap)?

options.text: The calendar widget fails to broadcast day selections to screen readers through automated aria-live polite region announcements
Modal dialog containers are normatively mandated to permanently trap keyboard focus while rendered in an active visual state
Focus cannot be moved away from the component using standard keyboard keys, and no instructions are provided for how to exit
The widget interface fails to provide an interactive mouse-clickable visual close icon in the top corner of the calendar grid

explanation: Under SC 2.1.2, if focus can be moved to a component using the keyboard, it must be possible to move focus away using standard keyboard commands (or clear instructions must explain how to exit). Trapping keyboard focus without a keyboard exit mechanism is a Level A failure.

distractorNotes.a: Live region announcements relate to dynamic notifications, not keyboard trap conformance under SC 2.1.2.
distractorNotes.b: Modal dialogs must contain focus while open, but they must allow the user to close or dismiss them (e.g. via Escape) to exit the trap.
distractorNotes.d: Mouse clickability is irrelevant to keyboard trap evaluation under SC 2.1.2.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.2 mandates that keyboard focus must not be trapped within any web component without a keyboard exit.

stem: A developer uses CSS flexbox `order` or CSS Grid layout properties to visually position a "Submit Order" button before billing fields, while leaving it last in the DOM source order. Why does this create a failure under WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.3 (Focus Order)?

options.text: CSS layout rules that modify visual positioning are strictly prohibited by HTML specifications from containing focusable elements
Screen readers automatically reorder their virtual reading buffers to match CSS visual layout, diverging from DOM sequence
User agents treat visually reordered flex items as off-screen content and suppress their computed accessible names in the tree
Keyboard navigation follows the DOM order, creating a confusing, non-sequential disconnect between visual focus and reading sequence

explanation: Under SC 2.4.3 (Focus Order, Level A), focusable components must receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. CSS flexbox order and Grid reposition elements visually on screen but do not alter the underlying DOM tab sequence, causing keyboard focus to jump unpredictably across the visual layout.

distractorNotes.a: CSS flexbox and Grid are fully valid on interactive forms; the failure arises specifically when visual order diverges from DOM focus sequence.
distractorNotes.b: Screen readers do not reorder their reading buffers based on CSS flexbox order; they continue following the underlying DOM order.
distractorNotes.c: CSS visual reordering does not hide elements or strip their computed accessible names in the accessibility tree.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3 requires that focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability.

stem: A web-based email client implements single-letter character key shortcuts (e.g., pressing "R" immediately initiates a reply, and "D" deletes the email). To conform to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.4 (Character Key Shortcuts, Level A), which mechanism must the application provide?

options.text: A mechanism to turn the shortcuts off, remap them to include non-printable modifiers, or make them active only when the component has focus
An automated audio chime notification played through system speakers whenever a single-key shortcut character is entered by the user
A modal confirmation dialog interrupting the workflow to confirm user intent before executing any single-key keyboard command action
A mandatory requirement forcing users to navigate through visual graphical menus using a physical mouse rather than keyboard presses

explanation: SC 2.1.4 requires that if a character key shortcut is implemented using only letters, punctuation, numbers, or symbols, at least one of the following is true: Turn off (a mechanism to turn the shortcut off), Remap (a mechanism to remap the shortcut to include modifier keys), or Active only on focus (the shortcut is only active when that component has focus).

distractorNotes.b: Audio beeps do not prevent accidental triggering by speech recognition or tremors.
distractorNotes.c: Confirmation dialogs on every keystroke introduce severe usability barriers rather than addressing shortcut remapping.
distractorNotes.d: Forcing mouse usage violates keyboard accessibility requirements under SC 2.1.1.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.4 specifies mechanisms to turn off, remap, or restrict single-character key shortcuts to focused states.

stem: A task management board allows users to drag task cards between status columns. To meet WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.7 (Dragging Movements, Level AA), what must the interface provide unless dragging is essential?

options.text: A keyboard navigation shortcut mechanism allowing users to move task cards using arrow keys or keystrokes
An alternative single-pointer mode of operation, such as clickable buttons or menus to move the item
A multi-touch or path-based gesture, such as a two-finger directional swipe, to execute card relocation
A timed hover dwell mechanism that automatically drops the dragged element after lingering over a target

explanation: Under SC 2.5.7 (Dragging Movements, Level AA), all functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential. Examples include providing 'Move Left / Move Right' buttons or an action dropdown menu.

distractorNotes.a: Keyboard navigation is required under SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard), but SC 2.5.7 specifically requires an alternative single-pointer method without dragging for pointer users who cannot drag.
distractorNotes.c: Path-based or multi-touch gestures still require precise motor control and fail SC 2.5.1 (Pointer Gestures) rather than providing a single-pointer alternative.
distractorNotes.d: Hover dwell mechanisms introduce timing barriers and unintended activations rather than providing explicit single-pointer controls.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7 requires a single-pointer alternative without dragging unless dragging is essential.

stem: An auditor evaluates an interactive icon button that measures 16 by 16 CSS pixels, which is smaller than the 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum requirement of SC 2.5.8. Under what circumstance does this button still pass the success criterion?

options.text: If the icon button visibly alters its background color when hovered by an active mouse pointer device
If the icon button provides a descriptive programmatic label using an explicit aria-label attribute
If the target offset spacing provides an unobstructed 24 CSS pixel diameter circle around the control
If the control is positioned exclusively within the persistent top header navigation bar of the page

explanation: SC 2.5.8 (Target Size (Minimum)) includes a Spacing exception: undersized targets pass if the target offset (a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle centered on the target bounding box) does not intersect any other target or target offset.

distractorNotes.a: Hover color change relates to visual state, not target dimensions or spacing.
distractorNotes.b: An accessible name satisfies SC 4.1.2, but does not provide physical motor target size compliance.
distractorNotes.d: Header placement confers no exemption under SC 2.5.8.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 defines the target offset spacing exception for interactive controls smaller than 24x24 CSS px.

stem: What is the primary purpose of Step 1 (Define the Evaluation Scope) in the Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM 1.0)?

options.text: To execute automated accessibility scanners against all available uniform resource locators in production
To recruit participants with diverse functional disabilities and conduct formal usability testing sessions
To refactor and remediate invalid HTML markup and non-compliant CSS style sheets across the web application
To establish the target web pages, target conformance level (A/AA/AAA), and accessibility support baseline

explanation: In WCAG-EM Step 1, the evaluator defines the scope of the evaluation: identifying the web application boundaries, defining the target conformance level (e.g. WCAG 2.2 Level AA), and agreeing on the accessibility support baseline (supported user agents and assistive technologies).

distractorNotes.a: Running automated tools occurs during Step 4 (Audit the Selected Sample), not Step 1.
distractorNotes.b: User testing is an optional complementary evaluation, not the normative definition of scope in Step 1.
distractorNotes.c: Code remediation is a development activity that occurs after an evaluation report is delivered.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM §4.1 Step 1 establishes evaluation scope, target conformance level, and accessibility support baseline.

stem: In WCAG-EM Step 2 (Explore the Target Website), which activity is explicitly performed by the evaluator to prepare for representative sample selection?

options.text: Identifying key web page types, essential functionalities, diverse web technologies, and interaction design patterns
Defining the evaluation scope boundaries, target conformance level, and agreed accessibility support baseline
Auditing all selected sample web pages against normative success criteria and recording accessibility defects
Selecting the structured representative pages and generating the complementary randomly chosen sample set

explanation: WCAG-EM Step 2 (Explore the Target Website) involves exploring the target website to identify its key web page types, essential user functionalities, diverse relied-upon technologies, and interaction design patterns in order to inform representative sample selection.

distractorNotes.b: Defining scope boundaries, target conformance level, and the accessibility support baseline occurs in WCAG-EM Step 1 (Define the Evaluation Scope).
distractorNotes.c: Auditing selected pages against success criteria and recording defects takes place in WCAG-EM Step 4 (Audit the Selected Sample).
distractorNotes.d: Selecting structured pages and generating the random sample set is executed in WCAG-EM Step 3 (Select a Representative Sample).

sourceNote: WCAG-EM §4.2 Step 2 focuses on identifying key page types, core functionality, and diverse technologies.

stem: When selecting a representative sample of web pages in WCAG-EM Step 3, what two distinct components must evaluators combine to ensure a balanced audit?

options.text: An automated crawler scan of all top-level URLs, combined with user-submitted accessibility helpdesk reports
A structured sample set of critical pages and complete processes, combined with a randomly selected sample set
A web analytics sample of high-traffic customer pages, combined with static marketing design landing templates
An exclusively randomized cross-section of URLs drawn directly from the production public sitemap index file

explanation: Under WCAG-EM Step 3 (Select a Representative Sample), the sample must include a structured sample set (common web pages, key user functionality, complete processes, diverse web technologies) supplemented by a randomly selected sample set to uncover unrepresented content.

distractorNotes.a: Automated scanner outputs and user helpdesk tickets do not constitute the structured sampling methodology required by WCAG-EM Step 3.
distractorNotes.c: High-traffic analytics pages and marketing mockups omit key transactional processes and randomized samples mandated by WCAG-EM.
distractorNotes.d: WCAG-EM mandates combining a structured sample with a random sample; an exclusively randomized sample fails to guarantee coverage of critical processes.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM §4.3 Step 3 mandates selecting a structured sample set supplemented by a randomly chosen sample.

stem: In WCAG-EM Step 4.2 (Audit complete processes), why is an evaluator required to evaluate an entire multi-step process (e.g., shopping cart checkout) rather than testing isolated pages individually?

options.text: Automated scanning engines are technically incapable of rendering web pages outside of sequential user checkout flows
Screen reader virtual buffers require a successful financial transaction event to initialize accessibility API trees
WCAG conformance cannot be claimed for a page if it is part of a process where any intermediate step fails to conform
Browser security models isolate session storage tokens differently when loading isolated web pages during evaluations

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.3 (Complete Processes) and WCAG-EM Step 4.2, when a web page is part of a series of steps in a process, all web pages in that process must conform for any conformance claim to be valid.

distractorNotes.a: Automated tools can scan isolated URLs regardless of whether they form part of a checkout workflow.
distractorNotes.b: Screen readers operate identically on individual pages and during checkout flows.
distractorNotes.d: Cookie caching is a browser networking implementation detail, not the rationale for process conformance.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.3 requires all pages in a process to conform for conformance claims.

stem: According to WCAG-EM Step 5 (Report the Evaluation Findings), which element must be included in a formal accessibility conformance report?

options.text: A legal warranty certifying that the website is completely indemnified against accessibility litigation and complaints
An automated compliance percentage score calculated from the proportion of passing rules across all scanned pages
Executable source code refactoring pull requests directly remediating each identified WCAG failure in the codebase
Clear documentation of the evaluation scope, WCAG version, conformance level, evaluated sample pages, and outcomes

explanation: WCAG-EM Step 5 specifies that a reporting deliverable must document the scope of the evaluation, the WCAG version and target level, dependencies, evaluated sample set, tools used, and detailed findings.

distractorNotes.a: WCAG-EM produces an objective technical evaluation report, not a legal indemnity or warranty against litigation.
distractorNotes.b: WCAG conformance is binary per criterion for full pages; WCAG-EM does not define or require a percentage compliance score.
distractorNotes.c: Code remediation pull requests are development activities that occur after the audit deliverable is completed.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM §4.5 Step 5 outlines required reporting components: scope, conformance level, sample pages, and findings.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.2 (Full Pages), can an organization claim conformance for an isolated UI widget or header section if other portions of the web page contain accessibility failures?

options.text: No, conformance is achieved only for full web pages and cannot be claimed for a part of a page
Yes, partial conformance claims are valid as long as the conforming region is marked with aria-label
Yes, organizations may claim conformance for any component that successfully passes automated tests
No, unless the non-conforming section is restricted exclusively to secondary responsive mobile views

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.2, conformance (and conformance levels) is for full web pages only, and cannot be claimed if part of the web page fails to conform.

distractorNotes.b: WCAG does not recognize partial page conformance claims on author-controlled pages.
distractorNotes.c: Automated pass rates do not override the normative requirement for full page conformance.
distractorNotes.d: Mobile rendering does not alter the full page conformance requirement.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.2 establishes that conformance applies only to full web pages.

stem: What is meant by "Accessibility-Supported Ways of Using Technologies" under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.4?

options.text: The web content technology is licensed under open-source software terms and published without restrictions
The web content technology is supported by users' assistive technologies as well as native user agents
The website deploys an automated machine-learning accessibility overlay script across all production pages
The web application functions with JavaScript execution completely disabled in client browser preferences

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.4, content must rely only on technologies that are accessibility-supported — meaning they are compatible with both users' assistive technologies (like screen readers) and user agents (browsers).

distractorNotes.a: Licensing models (open source vs proprietary) have no bearing on technical accessibility support.
distractorNotes.c: AI overlays are third-party scripts that do not define accessibility-supported technology usage.
distractorNotes.d: JavaScript is an accessibility-supported technology when coded using semantic WAI-ARIA and HTML standards.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.4 defines accessibility-supported technology usage in user agents.

stem: Why do professional accessibility evaluation guidelines state that automated testing tools can only detect approximately 30 to 40 percent of WCAG accessibility barriers?

options.text: Automated scanners cannot parse modern CSS style rules or calculate computed cascading style sheet properties on web pages
Automated testing engines are restricted to evaluating websites that are authored in the English language and Latin alphabet
Automated tools cannot evaluate subjective semantic appropriateness, such as whether alternative text accurately conveys image context
Browser security sandboxes systematically prevent automated testing extensions from querying the document object model tree

explanation: Automated tools can verify programmatic existence (such as checking whether an img element has an alt attribute), but cannot judge contextual human meaning (such as whether the alt text accurately conveys the image's purpose), logical reading order, or custom widget usability.

distractorNotes.a: Modern automated test runners evaluate computed CSS styles and cascade rules.
distractorNotes.b: Automated rules engines evaluate DOM nodes regardless of the natural language of the text.
distractorNotes.d: Automated testing engines operate with full programmatic access to DOM structures and accessibility trees.

sourceNote: W3C WAI guidance on selecting evaluation tools explains the scope and limitations of automated accessibility testing.

stem: An automated accessibility scanner flags an image of a complex sales chart with alt="chart" as a "Pass" for WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content). In accessibility auditing terminology, what does this outcome represent?

options.text: True positive
options.hintText: an automated tool correctly identifies an actual accessibility barrier

options.text: False positive
options.hintText: an automated tool incorrectly flags conforming content as an accessibility failure

options.text: True negative
options.hintText: an automated tool correctly identifies conforming content as passing

options.text: False negative
options.hintText: an automated tool fails to report an actual accessibility violation that is present

explanation: A false negative occurs when an actual accessibility failure exists in the content (the alt text is completely inadequate for a complex chart), but the automated tool fails to report it as a defect because it only verified that the alt attribute was present.

distractorNotes.a: A true positive occurs when a real defect is correctly identified and flagged by the tool.
distractorNotes.b: A false positive occurs when an automated tool incorrectly flags valid, conforming content as a failure.
distractorNotes.c: The content fails SC 1.1.1, so this outcome is not a true negative result.

sourceNote: W3C WAI evaluation tools resources define false positives and false negatives in automated conformance testing.

stem: What is the primary objective of the W3C Accessibility Conformance Testing (ACT) Rules Community Group?

options.text: To develop harmonized test rules that ensure consistent interpretation and evaluation of WCAG across different automated and manual testing tools
To supersede the normative WCAG 2.2 recommendation with a legally binding automated algorithmic validation protocol across member nations
To operate a commercial certification program that endorses proprietary commercial accessibility evaluation software products and vendors
To establish an international web standard mandating that public web applications eliminate all custom client-side JavaScript components

explanation: The W3C ACT Rules Community Group writes standardized, atomic test rules to ensure that automated testing tools and manual auditing methodologies interpret and test WCAG criteria consistently across vendors and testing organizations.

distractorNotes.b: ACT rules do not replace WCAG; they define specific test procedures to assess WCAG success criteria.
distractorNotes.c: ACT is an open W3C community standard effort, not a commercial vendor certification scheme.
distractorNotes.d: ACT rules evaluate web content, rather than prohibiting JavaScript technologies.

sourceNote: W3C ACT Rules Community Group defines standardized test rules to harmonize accessibility evaluations.

stem: When inspecting an interactive custom component in browser developer tools, why is checking the computed Accessibility Tree more reliable than inspecting the raw HTML source code alone?

options.text: The accessibility tree calculates the exact color contrast luminosity ratios and font weights of all rendered text elements on the screen
The accessibility tree reveals the computed role, name, states, and properties actually exposed to assistive technologies via platform APIs
The accessibility tree automatically injects missing form input label elements and repairs invalid ARIA attributes in the live DOM source
The accessibility tree emulates keyboard focus movement by forcing tab stop coordinates across elements with negative tabindex

explanation: The browser accessibility tree shows the final computed accessibility properties (role, name, description, states) passed to platform accessibility APIs (e.g. MSAA, UI Automation, NSAccessibility, AT-SPI), reflecting all HTML, CSS, and ARIA interactions.

distractorNotes.a: Color contrast ratios are displayed in style and color inspection panels, not the accessibility tree.
distractorNotes.c: Developer tools inspect properties; they do not alter or fix author markup on the live page.
distractorNotes.d: The accessibility tree reflects semantic roles and properties; it does not force or simulate sequential keyboard tab ring movements.

sourceNote: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 §1.4 describes the platform accessibility tree generated by user agents for assistive technologies.

stem: An interactive button element is defined as `<button id="btn" aria-labelledby="label1" aria-label="Cancel Order" title="Dismiss">Submit Order</button>`. According to the W3C Accessible Name and Description Computation (AccName 1.2) algorithm, what source takes highest precedence to establish the button's accessible name?

options.text: The inner text content of the button subtree ("Submit Order")
The programmatic text string provided in aria-label ("Cancel Order")
The element referenced by the aria-labelledby attribute ("label1")
The advisory text string provided in the HTML title attribute ("Dismiss")

explanation: Under the W3C AccName 1.2 specification, aria-labelledby has highest precedence in name computation. If aria-labelledby is present and valid, it overrides aria-label, native subtree text ("Submit Order"), and the title attribute.

distractorNotes.a: Subtree text content is only used if aria-labelledby and aria-label are absent or do not compute.
distractorNotes.b: aria-label is evaluated only if aria-labelledby is not present or yields an empty string.
distractorNotes.d: The title attribute has the lowest precedence among naming mechanisms in the AccName algorithm.

sourceNote: W3C AccName 1.2 §4.3 defines the precedence order for accessible name computation: aria-labelledby precedes aria-label.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.5 (Non-Interference), which specific group of success criteria must be satisfied by all technologies on a page, even when relying on conforming alternative versions?

options.text: SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), SC 1.4.4 Resize Text, and SC 1.4.10 Reflow for responsive layouts
SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context), and SC 3.1.1 Language of Page
SC 2.4.6 Headings and Labels, SC 2.5.3 Label in Name, and SC 3.3.2 Form Labels or Field Instructions
SC 1.4.2 Audio Control, SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap, SC 2.3.1 Three Flashes, and SC 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide

explanation: Conformance Requirement 5.2.5 (Non-Interference) mandates that non-conforming content must not interfere with the rest of the page. All content must satisfy five specific criteria: 1.4.2 (Audio Control), 2.1.1 (Keyboard), 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap), 2.3.1 (Three Flashes), and 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide).

distractorNotes.a: Contrast, text resize, and reflow are not part of the non-interference requirement set.
distractorNotes.b: Semantic structure and page language criteria can be satisfied by conforming alternative versions.
distractorNotes.c: Heading labels and instructions do not cause catastrophic operational blocking under Non-Interference.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.5 defines the non-interference criteria: 1.4.2, 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.2.2, and 2.3.1.

stem: When testing an interactive custom ARIA widget such as a tree view (role="tree") or slider (role="slider") with NVDA, why must an auditor ensure NVDA switches to Focus Mode (or toggle with NVDA+Space)?

options.text: Browse Mode mutes synthesizer speech output during user interactions with ARIA roles
In Browse Mode, NVDA intercepts arrow keys for virtual navigation instead of passing them to the widget
Focus Mode is required because modern browsers block keyboard focus on ARIA elements in Browse Mode
Browse Mode forces all composite ARIA widgets to render as static layout graphics in the DOM tree

explanation: In Browse Mode, NVDA intercepts standard navigation keys like arrow keys to move its virtual cursor across content. To operate custom ARIA widgets requiring arrow keys, NVDA must enter Focus Mode so keystrokes pass directly to the browser and widget event handlers.

distractorNotes.a: Browse Mode does not mute speech output; it verbalizes text at the virtual cursor position.
distractorNotes.c: Browsers manage keyboard focus through tabindex and the DOM regardless of the active NVDA mode.
distractorNotes.d: Browse Mode does not alter ARIA widget roles or convert them into static graphic representations.

sourceNote: NVDA User Guide §5.5 explains Focus Mode passes keys to the app while Browse Mode intercepts keys.

stem: During an accessibility audit using NVDA, which tool within NVDA can an evaluator enable to display a floating visual window showing all text spoken by the speech synthesizer in real time?

options.text: NVDA Python Developer Console
options.hintText: interactive console for inspecting internal NVDA variables and debugging code

options.text: Windows Narrator Live Transcript
options.hintText: utility panel displaying real-time text transcription of Windows Narrator speech

options.text: NVDA Speech Viewer
options.hintText: floating window displaying real-time text transcription of speech spoken by NVDA

options.text: Review Cursor Object Inspector
options.hintText: utility dialog providing diagnostic information about the navigator object

explanation: The NVDA Speech Viewer displays a floating window showing the exact text currently being spoken by NVDA. This utility enables sighted or hard of hearing auditors to verify speech output, confirm pronunciation, and copy announcements for defect reports.

distractorNotes.a: The Python Console is a development tool used for inspecting internal objects and debugging scripts.
distractorNotes.b: Windows Narrator is a separate screen reader built into Windows rather than an NVDA feature.
distractorNotes.d: The Review Cursor is a navigation mechanism for reading screen content, not a speech transcript tool.

sourceNote: NVDA User Guide §11.1 describes the Speech Viewer floating window for displaying spoken synthesizer text.

stem: An accessibility evaluator needs to inspect dynamic status text that does not receive keyboard focus and is skipped by Browse Mode. Which NVDA feature allows navigating screen objects independently of system keyboard focus?

options.text: Review Cursor and Object Navigation
options.hintText: navigates screen content and object hierarchies independently of system focus in NVDA

options.text: Virtual PC Cursor Navigation
options.hintText: moves system keyboard focus through web page content in JAWS

options.text: Touch Cursor Mode
options.hintText: simulates touch navigation using arrow keys in JAWS

options.text: Browse Mode Document Search
options.hintText: searches for matching text strings in the virtual buffer in NVDA

explanation: NVDA Review Cursor and Object Navigation allow auditors to inspect content, off-screen text, and accessible properties of objects without shifting system focus, typically operated via numeric keypad commands in desktop keyboard layout.

distractorNotes.b: Tab and Shift+Tab move system keyboard focus directly rather than reviewing objects independently.
distractorNotes.c: Touch Cursor is a JAWS feature rather than an NVDA navigation mode.
distractorNotes.d: Document search finds matching text strings in Browse Mode but does not navigate arbitrary screen objects.

sourceNote: NVDA User Guide §5.2 outlines Reviewing Text and Object Navigation using the review cursor.

stem: When using NVDA in Browse Mode to audit a complex online application form, which single-letter quick navigation key moves the virtual cursor specifically to the next checkbox on the web page?

options.text: Key C
options.hintText: moves to the next combo box in NVDA Browse Mode

options.text: Key F
options.hintText: moves to the next form field in NVDA Browse Mode

options.text: Key K
options.hintText: moves to the next link in NVDA Browse Mode

options.text: Key X
options.hintText: moves to the next checkbox in NVDA Browse Mode

explanation: In NVDA Browse Mode, single-letter navigation key X jumps to the next checkbox (and Shift+X to previous). Key F jumps to any form field, Key C jumps to comboboxes, and Key K jumps to links.

distractorNotes.a: Key C jumps to the next combobox in NVDA Browse Mode.
distractorNotes.b: Key F moves to the next form field of any type rather than checkboxes specifically.
distractorNotes.c: Key K jumps to the next hyperlink on the page.

sourceNote: NVDA User Guide §5.5.1 lists quick navigation keys: X moves to the next checkbox.

stem: While auditing an older web page with NVDA, an evaluator observes that an HTML <table> element used purely for visual formatting is announced as a 4-column data table. How should the evaluator verify whether NVDA is treating the table as presentation?

options.text: Ensure NVDA Document Formatting settings have table announcements silenced
Inspect whether browser developer tools flag the layout table as an invalid HTML structure
Check if pressing F5 refreshes the DOM to strip layout tables automatically
Check if NVDA reports dimensions or if role='presentation' removes table semantics

explanation: NVDA uses heuristics to distinguish layout tables from data tables. When an author adds role='presentation' or role='none' to a table element, screen readers strip row, column, and grid semantics, treating child cells as generic text containers.

distractorNotes.a: Silencing table announcements in preferences suppresses feedback on legitimate data tables.
distractorNotes.b: Browser devtools validate HTML syntax, but layout tables are valid HTML and are not flagged as syntax errors.
distractorNotes.c: Pressing F5 reloads the web page but does not alter semantic markup or table heuristics.

sourceNote: WAI Tutorials on Tables note presentation tables must use role='presentation' to strip table semantics.

stem: During an audit in JAWS, an alert notification is spoken quickly and disappears before the evaluator can document its exact wording. Which JAWS command opens the Speech History window to review recently spoken synthesizer output?

options.text: Pressing Insert + Spacebar followed by H
options.hintText: opens the Speech History window in JAWS to review recent announcements

options.text: Pressing Insert + F7 followed by Enter
options.hintText: opens the Links List dialog and activates the selected link in JAWS

options.text: Pressing Ctrl + Shift + V in the browser
options.hintText: pastes plain unformatted text from the clipboard in desktop applications

options.text: Pressing Insert + Escape to refresh screen
options.hintText: refreshes the active screen or virtual buffer in JAWS

explanation: In JAWS, pressing the layered keystroke Insert + Spacebar followed by H opens the JAWS Speech History window, allowing the auditor to review, select, and copy the most recent strings spoken by the synthesizer.

distractorNotes.b: Insert + F7 opens the Links List dialog in JAWS.
distractorNotes.c: Ctrl + Shift + V pastes unformatted clipboard text in browsers.
distractorNotes.d: Insert + Escape refreshes the current screen without displaying speech history.

sourceNote: Freedom Scientific JAWS commands cite Insert+Spacebar, H to display speech history.

stem: When testing web content that cannot receive keyboard focus in JAWS, what mode enables navigating visual screen regions and inspecting layout structures using arrow keys without moving the system mouse?

options.text: Virtual PC Forms Mode
Screen Review Document Mode
JAWS Touch Cursor
Braille Line Tracking Mode

explanation: The JAWS Touch Cursor (activated with Shift + Numpad Plus) enables users and auditors to navigate screen elements and touch-friendly controls using arrow keys as if touching the screen, even if elements are not standard focusable HTML controls.

distractorNotes.a: Virtual PC Forms Mode routes keystrokes directly to form fields for text entry.
distractorNotes.b: Screen Review Document Mode is not a recognized JAWS navigation mode.
distractorNotes.d: Braille Line Tracking Mode controls refreshable braille displays rather than screen inspection.

sourceNote: Freedom Scientific JAWS documentation explains Touch Cursor mode for navigating on-screen elements.

stem: While auditing a complex data table in JAWS, an evaluator wants to hear the current cell's column and row header information along with its coordinates. Which keystroke combination accomplishes this in JAWS?

options.text: Ctrl + Alt + Left Arrow
Ctrl + Alt + Numpad 5
Insert + Shift + T
Alt + Delete + Space

explanation: In JAWS, pressing Ctrl + Alt + Numpad 5 (or Insert + Shift + Numpad 5 in laptop layout) announces the current table cell contents, its associated row and column headers, and its grid coordinates.

distractorNotes.a: Ctrl + Alt + Left Arrow moves focus to the previous cell in the current row.
distractorNotes.c: Insert + Shift + T is not the standard JAWS table cell identification shortcut.
distractorNotes.d: Alt + Delete announces the cursor position relative to the active window margins.

sourceNote: Freedom Scientific JAWS table commands cite Ctrl+Alt+Numpad 5 to read current cell and headers.

stem: In JAWS, how does Auto Forms Mode typically behave when an evaluator tabs from static paragraph text into an HTML <input type='text'> edit field?

options.text: JAWS plays a sound and enters Forms Mode, routing typing directly to the input
JAWS requires the evaluator to manually press Enter or Spacebar to enter Forms Mode
JAWS silences virtual navigation keys but keeps the Virtual PC Cursor active until typing starts
JAWS announces the field label and automatically routes keyboard focus to the submit button

explanation: By default, JAWS operates in Auto Forms Mode. When focus lands on an edit field via Tab, JAWS plays a distinctive sound (pop) and switches from the Virtual PC Cursor to Forms Mode so keystrokes type directly into the field.

distractorNotes.b: Manually pressing Enter or Spacebar is required in Manual Forms Mode, whereas Auto Forms Mode activates automatically.
distractorNotes.c: Auto Forms Mode deactivates the Virtual PC Cursor immediately upon entering the field so keystrokes type directly into the input.
distractorNotes.d: JAWS routes focus to the active input control itself, not to the form submit button.

sourceNote: Freedom Scientific documentation explains Auto Forms Mode activating upon navigating into form controls.

stem: An evaluator is testing a web-based spreadsheet application that relies on single-letter keyboard shortcuts. In JAWS, which shortcut temporarily toggles Virtual PC Cursor Quick Keys off so letter keys are passed directly to the web app?

options.text: Insert + F4
options.hintText: closes and unloads JAWS from the operating system

options.text: Insert + Tab
options.hintText: announces current focus or active form control state in JAWS

options.text: Insert + F2
options.hintText: opens the Run JAWS Manager dialog listing active configurations

options.text: Insert + Z
options.hintText: temporarily toggles Virtual PC Cursor Quick Keys on or off in JAWS

explanation: In JAWS, pressing Insert + Z toggles the Virtual PC Cursor on or off (or disables Navigation Quick Keys). When disabled, pressing letters like H, T, or F sends keystrokes directly to the web application instead of triggering screen reader quick navigation.

distractorNotes.a: Insert + F4 closes and exits JAWS completely.
distractorNotes.b: Insert + Tab repeats the currently focused element and its state.
distractorNotes.c: Insert + F2 opens the JAWS Run JAWS Manager dialog.

sourceNote: Freedom Scientific JAWS commands document Insert+Z for toggling Virtual PC Cursor in web apps.

stem: When auditing whether all sections of an enterprise web portal are wrapped in appropriate ARIA landmarks using JAWS, which shortcut displays a dialog listing all landmarks and regions on the page?

options.text: Insert + F3
Insert + Ctrl + R
Insert + Shift + L
Insert + Alt + M

explanation: In JAWS, pressing Insert + Ctrl + R displays the Regions/Landmarks dialog, allowing an evaluator to view, count, and navigate between all defined landmarks (<header>, <main>, <nav>, role='region', etc.) on the page.

distractorNotes.a: Insert + F3 is not the JAWS regions dialog command.
distractorNotes.c: Insert + Shift + L is not a standard JAWS landmark list shortcut.
distractorNotes.d: Insert + Alt + M does not open the landmarks dialog in JAWS.

sourceNote: Freedom Scientific documentation notes Insert+Ctrl+R displays the JAWS Select a Region/Landmark dialog.

stem: An accessibility evaluator using VoiceOver on macOS wants a visual caption box on screen displaying spoken text for documenting audit issues. Which VoiceOver feature should be enabled?

options.text: macOS Voice Control Dictation Bubble
options.hintText: floating interface providing visual feedback for spoken speech recognition commands

options.text: Safari Web Inspector Console Drawer
options.hintText: browser developer tool panel logging runtime JavaScript events and console messages

options.text: VoiceOver Caption Panel
options.hintText: floating visual window displaying on-screen text transcripts of VoiceOver speech

options.text: VoiceOver Speech History Window
options.hintText: utility window opened via VO + H then H displaying past spoken announcements

explanation: The VoiceOver Caption Panel (configured in VoiceOver Utility > Visuals > Panels) displays a resizable high-contrast window showing the exact text spoken by VoiceOver, making it straightforward for auditors to visually monitor announcements and capture screenshots.

distractorNotes.a: Dictation Bubble displays recognized speech input words rather than screen reader spoken output.
distractorNotes.b: Web Inspector Console displays JavaScript errors and console logs rather than VoiceOver speech.
distractorNotes.d: The Speech History menu displays past announcements in a modal list, but does not provide a floating real-time visual caption window.

sourceNote: Apple VoiceOver Guide describes enabling the Caption Panel under Visuals to display spoken text.

stem: When testing an HTML data table with VoiceOver on macOS in Safari, an auditor notices that row and column header titles are not spoken when arrowing into cells. What VoiceOver configuration setting should the auditor check?

options.text: VoiceOver Utility > Web > 'Always speak web page descriptions aloud'
VoiceOver Utility > Navigation > 'Group items when moving in DOM tree'
VoiceOver Utility > Verbosity > 'Announce table headers' in Web options
Safari Preferences > Advanced > 'Disable native table semantics in DOM'

explanation: VoiceOver includes verbosity settings under VoiceOver Utility > Verbosity. Under Web options, auditors can configure how tables are read, including whether column and row headers are announced automatically when moving into table cells.

distractorNotes.a: Web page descriptions setting controls page summary announcements, not table header repetition.
distractorNotes.b: Grouping controls DOM grouping behavior during linear reading rather than table header speech.
distractorNotes.d: Safari has no preference setting to disable native table semantics.

sourceNote: Apple VoiceOver User Guide describes Verbosity settings for web content, including table header announcements.

stem: An evaluator uses the VoiceOver Web Rotor (VO + U) on macOS to check page structure, but the 'Landmarks' panel does not appear when arrowing through rotor categories. How can the evaluator restore it?

options.text: Press VO + Shift + U to dynamically toggle unselected rotor categories
Open VoiceOver Utility > Web > Web Rotor and check the Landmarks option
Add an aria-rotor='landmarks' attribute to the document body element
Press VO + Command + Shift + R to reset all system rotor preferences

explanation: The VoiceOver Web Rotor can be customized in VoiceOver Utility > Web > Web Rotor. If a category such as Landmarks, Tables, or Form Controls is unchecked in this list, it will not appear when VO + U is opened.

distractorNotes.a: VO + Shift + U does not toggle rotor categories; rotor options are configured in VoiceOver Utility.
distractorNotes.c: There is no HTML or ARIA attribute named aria-rotor.
distractorNotes.d: VO + Command + Shift + R is not a valid VoiceOver reset shortcut.

sourceNote: Apple VoiceOver Guide explains customizing rotor options in VoiceOver Utility > Web > Web Rotor.

stem: In VoiceOver on macOS with Safari, an auditor reaches an HTML <table> or <iframe> and VoiceOver announces 'Table, 4 columns, 5 rows'. What key command must the auditor press to move focus inside the container to read its cells?

options.text: Pressing VO + Spacebar
options.hintText: activates or clicks the currently focused element in VoiceOver

options.text: Pressing VO + J
options.hintText: jumps to the linked or enclosing item in VoiceOver

options.text: Pressing VO + Return
options.hintText: initiates text editing or submits a form control in VoiceOver

options.text: Pressing VO + Shift + Down Arrow
options.hintText: interacts with an item or moves into a container in VoiceOver

explanation: macOS VoiceOver uses an explicit hierarchical interaction model. When encountering complex composite elements like tables, lists, scroll areas, and iframes, the user must press VO + Shift + Down Arrow to interact with items inside, and VO + Shift + Up Arrow to stop interacting.

distractorNotes.a: VO + Spacebar activates links, buttons, or checkboxes rather than interacting with compound containers.
distractorNotes.b: VO + J jumps to the linked element or container without entering interaction mode.
distractorNotes.c: VO + Return opens links or enters text edit fields in certain applications.

sourceNote: Apple VoiceOver User Guide describes using VO+Shift+Down Arrow to interact with items in an area or table.

stem: While conducting an accessibility audit on an iPhone using VoiceOver, an auditor needs to verify that the interface can be navigated solely by audio without visual cues. What touch gesture toggles the Screen Curtain on or off?

options.text: Triple-tapping with three fingers on the screen
Double-tapping with two fingers anywhere on the screen
Swiping down with four fingers from the top bezel
Long-pressing with three fingers for five seconds

explanation: On iOS with VoiceOver enabled, triple-tapping with three fingers turns the Screen Curtain on or off, blacking out the screen so auditors can test non-visual operation. (Double-tapping with three fingers toggles speech on or off).

distractorNotes.b: Two-finger double tap is the 'Magic Tap' (starts or pauses media and answers calls).
distractorNotes.c: Four-finger swipe switches between open apps on iOS devices.
distractorNotes.d: Three-finger long press does not toggle Screen Curtain.

sourceNote: Apple iPhone User Guide defines VoiceOver gestures: triple-tap with three fingers toggles the Screen Curtain.

stem: When testing a mobile web list item with custom swipe actions (such as 'Archive' or 'Delete') in VoiceOver on iOS, how does an evaluator trigger those contextual actions?

options.text: Performing a rapid three-finger flick to the left side of the screen
Rotating the rotor to 'Actions' and swiping up or down with one finger
Swiping horizontally with two fingers across the list item to reveal action buttons
Double-tapping and holding on the item to trigger a standard context menu

explanation: On iOS VoiceOver, custom element actions appear in the Rotor under 'Actions'. The user rotates two fingers to select 'Actions' and swipes up or down with one finger to hear each action, double-tapping to activate.

distractorNotes.a: A three-finger flick scrolls pages rather than triggering element action menus.
distractorNotes.c: Two-finger horizontal swiping is a standard touch gesture that VoiceOver intercepts rather than passing to custom swipe actions.
distractorNotes.d: Double-tap and hold simulates a long press, but VoiceOver custom list item actions are accessed via the Actions rotor.

sourceNote: Apple iOS VoiceOver documentation details the Actions rotor item for activating contextual actions.

stem: When auditing mobile web pages on Android with Google TalkBack, what standard multi-finger gesture allows an evaluator to cycle through reading controls (such as Headings, Links, or Controls)?

options.text: Swiping up with three fingers or swiping down with three fingers
Double-tapping with four fingers simultaneously on the screen
Pinching inward with two fingers while pressing volume down
Swiping left with two fingers from the right screen bezel

explanation: In modern TalkBack (version 9.1+), swiping up with three fingers or swiping down with three fingers cycles through reading controls like Characters, Words, Lines, Headings, Links, and Controls.

distractorNotes.b: Four-finger double tap is not a standard TalkBack navigation command.
distractorNotes.c: Pinching with two fingers does not adjust reading controls; it zooms content.
distractorNotes.d: Two-finger swipe left or right scrolls content horizontally in TalkBack.

sourceNote: Google TalkBack Help outlines using a three-finger swipe up or down to cycle through reading controls.

stem: When using the Colour Contrast Analyser (CCA) eyedropper tool to evaluate small anti-aliased text rendered on a textured or solid background, what is the best practice for sampling the text color?

options.text: Sample the outer blurred fringe pixels of the font stroke where smoothing blends
Sample an average of the entire web page viewport color histogram using a browser tool
Sample the solid center core pixel of the font glyph stroke at high screen magnification
Sample the computed color value directly from the browser Computed Styles panel without eyedropper checks

explanation: Anti-aliasing creates gradient transition pixels around glyph edges. Sampling edge pixels skews the reading toward the background color. Evaluators must magnify the screen and sample the solid interior core pixel of the font stroke to measure the intended foreground contrast.

distractorNotes.a: Sampling outer fringe pixels produces inaccurate contrast ratios because those pixels blend with the background.
distractorNotes.b: Viewport color histograms measure overall page palette rather than specific text-to-background contrast.
distractorNotes.d: Relying on computed CSS color values fails to capture gradient backgrounds, image textures, or anti-aliasing blending.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 1.4.3 explains measuring contrast for anti-aliased text by sampling pixels within stroke core.

stem: During an audit of an e-commerce checkout form, an evaluator enters invalid data into the 'Zip Code' field. The input border turns red, but no text message, icon, or formatting change appears. Why does this violate WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 (Use of Color)?

options.text: The red border fails to satisfy the 4.5:1 minimum contrast requirement for body text
Input error styling must include an aria-invalid='true' attribute before visual borders can be rendered
HTML form fields are prohibited from modifying CSS border colors upon validation failure
Color is used as the sole visual means of conveying that an input error has occurred

explanation: WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.1 (Use of Color, Level A) requires that color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element. Adding an error icon, text message, or bold outline provides a non-color visual cue.

distractorNotes.a: Input borders are user interface components evaluated under SC 1.4.11 (3:1), not SC 1.4.3 (4.5:1).
distractorNotes.b: SC 1.4.1 governs visual presentation of information; programmatic attributes like aria-invalid are evaluated under SC 4.1.2.
distractorNotes.c: CSS border color modification is allowed as long as an additional non-color indicator is provided.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 requires that color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information or error states.

stem: An evaluator tests a button's keyboard focus indicator under WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast). The button background is dark blue (#002244) on a white page (#FFFFFF). When focused, a 2px solid light blue outline (#66AAFF) appears around the button. What must the outline contrast against by at least 3:1?

options.text: Against the inner text label and icon rendered inside the button element
Directly against neighboring interactive button and link components positioned on the web page
Against the operating system and browser default gray focus ring color
Against adjacent background colors (the button background and/or the white page)

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast) and SC 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance), the focus indicator must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors (such as the outer background of the page or the inner background of the focused component).

distractorNotes.a: Focus outlines surround the component boundary and must contrast against adjacent backgrounds, not internal text.
distractorNotes.b: Focus indicators do not need to contrast against other unrelated buttons on the page.
distractorNotes.c: WCAG criteria evaluate the author's custom style against page backgrounds, not against default browser rings.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires 3:1 contrast for user interface component states against adjacent colors.

stem: An evaluator audits a standalone pie chart graphic illustrating company market share. Three adjacent slices use pastel shades of yellow, light green, and light blue with contrast ratios of 1.4:1 between them and no separating lines. Why does this fail WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast)?

options.text: Data visualizations and pie charts are classified as complex graphics and are fully exempt from SC 1.4.11
Vector charts only require 3:1 contrast against the page background, regardless of contrast between adjacent data slices
Visual parts required to identify graphical objects must achieve at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors
Data graphics satisfy contrast requirements automatically if an accessible name is provided via aria-label

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 requires that visual information required to identify parts of graphical objects (like slices of a pie chart) have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors, or use a contrasting 3:1 border or separator line.

distractorNotes.a: Complex graphics are not exempt from SC 1.4.11; visual boundaries required to distinguish data slices must meet 3:1 or use borders.
distractorNotes.b: SC 1.4.11 requires 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors for visual parts required to identify parts of graphical objects, including neighboring slices.
distractorNotes.d: Accessible names satisfy SC 1.1.1 and 4.1.2, but do not satisfy visual contrast requirements under SC 1.4.11.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 mandates 3:1 contrast for graphical objects required to understand content.

stem: When testing a responsive web page for conformance with WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow), an evaluator configures the desktop browser viewport to 1280 CSS pixels wide and zooms to 400%. What is the effective CSS viewport width being evaluated?

options.text: 320 CSS pixels
480 CSS pixels
640 CSS pixels
1024 CSS pixels

explanation: 1280 CSS pixels divided by 400% zoom (scale factor of 4) equals 320 CSS pixels. WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 requires that content reflow without two-dimensional scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels for vertically scrolling content.

distractorNotes.b: 480 CSS pixels corresponds to approximately 267% zoom at 1280 CSS pixels.
distractorNotes.c: 640 CSS pixels corresponds to 200% zoom at 1280 CSS pixels.
distractorNotes.d: 1024 CSS pixels corresponds to 125% zoom at 1280 CSS pixels.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 requires reflow at a width of 320 CSS pixels, equivalent to 400% zoom at 1280px width.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (Reflow), which type of web content is explicitly exempted from the requirement to avoid horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS pixels?

options.text: Multi-column article blogs, editorial news posts, and standard marketing copy paragraphs
Complex multi-dimensional data tables, maps, and video player control toolbars
Primary website navigation headers, skip links, and full footer legal copyright sections
User registration forms, multi-step checkout questionnaires, and customer account login portals

explanation: SC 1.4.10 provides an exception for content where two-dimensional layout is essential to its presentation or usage, such as data tables with multiple columns, geographic maps, diagrams, code blocks, and games.

distractorNotes.a: Blog articles and text paragraphs must reflow into a single column without horizontal scrolling.
distractorNotes.c: Navigation menus and footer blocks must reflow without requiring horizontal scrolling.
distractorNotes.d: Form fields and checkout workflows are required to reflow into a responsive vertical layout.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 lists exceptions where 2D layout is essential: data tables, maps, diagrams, and games.

stem: When testing an application for WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.4 (Resize Text, Level AA), why must an evaluator specifically test 'Zoom Text Only' (such as in Firefox) in addition to full browser page zoom?

options.text: SC 1.4.4 requires text to scale up to 200% without assistive tech and without containers clipping or truncating text
Browser page zoom is classified as external assistive technology and cannot be accepted for WCAG conformance claims
Responsive layouts that adapt at 400% zoom satisfy both reflow and text resizing requirements automatically
Text-only zoom evaluates SC 1.4.12 text spacing overrides rather than SC 1.4.4 font enlargement

explanation: SC 1.4.4 requires text to be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality. While page zoom scales layout boxes together with text, 'Zoom Text Only' scales only font sizes inside fixed-height containers, exposing overflow clippings and overlaps.

distractorNotes.b: Browser page zoom is a standard user agent feature, not external assistive technology.
distractorNotes.c: Passing reflow at 400% page zoom does not satisfy SC 1.4.4, which specifically requires container resilience when font sizes alone are increased.
