distractorNotes.d: SC 1.4.12 evaluates specific spacing metrics (line height, letter spacing), whereas text-only zoom evaluates SC 1.4.4 font resizing up to 200%.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 1.4.4 notes that text-only resize verifies containers adapt without truncating text.

stem: An evaluator applies a standard WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 (Text Spacing) bookmarklet to test content resilience. Which four exact CSS text styling metrics must the web page accommodate without loss of content or functionality?

options.text: Paragraph font weight 700, margin spacing 24px, line height 1.8 times font size, and padding 16px across text containers
Text indent 2em, uppercase text transform, line height 2.5 times font size, and expanded font stretch across typography
Line height 1.5, paragraph spacing 2 times font size, letter spacing 0.12 times font size, and word spacing 0.16 times font size
Line height 2.0, column count 2, letter spacing 0.25 times font size, and word spacing 0.5 times font size across layout

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 specifies exact minimum metrics: line height (line spacing) to at least 1.5 times font size, spacing following paragraphs to at least 2 times font size, letter spacing to at least 0.12 times font size, and word spacing to at least 0.16 times font size.

distractorNotes.a: SC 1.4.12 does not specify font weight, margin, or padding dimensions.
distractorNotes.b: Text indent and text transform are not part of the text spacing metrics.
distractorNotes.d: These multipliers exceed the specific thresholds defined in SC 1.4.12.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 defines exact metrics: line height 1.5x, paragraph space 2x, letter space 0.12x, word space 0.16x.

stem: While auditing an icon button in Windows Contrast Mode (Forced Colors Mode), an evaluator notices the icon vanishes completely. Inspecting CSS reveals the icon was rendered via background-image: url('search.svg'). Why does this issue occur?

options.text: Forced Colors Mode drops vector SVG assets while preserving raster PNG and JPEG background images
Browsers suppress background images only when the calculated contrast ratio of the icon falls below 3:1
Forced Colors Mode overrides color properties but keeps background-image declarations unless forced-color-adjust is none
Forced Colors Mode strips CSS background images, requiring inline SVG elements or high contrast media queries

explanation: In Forced Colors Mode (such as Windows High Contrast Mode), browsers override author colors and strip CSS background images to ensure high-contrast readability. Meaningful icons rendered as CSS backgrounds disappear unless authored using inline SVG, tags, or forced-color-adjust: none.

distractorNotes.a: Forced Colors Mode strips all CSS background images regardless of whether they are vector SVG or raster images.
distractorNotes.b: Background images are stripped by default across the board to ensure text contrast, not selectively based on contrast calculation.
distractorNotes.c: By default, Forced Colors Mode strips background-image declarations; forced-color-adjust: none preserves them rather than stripping them.

sourceNote: WAI page styling tutorials explain that forced colors mode strips CSS background images, hiding non-inline icons.

stem: When hovering over an information icon, a descriptive tooltip pops up covering adjacent text. According to WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus), what must the web page provide to satisfy the 'Dismissible' requirement?

options.text: A requirement that moving the mouse pointer at least 20 pixels away from the trigger immediately dismisses the tooltip
A mechanism such as the Escape key to dismiss the tooltip without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus
An automatic three-second countdown timer that dismisses the tooltip window without requiring user input
A separate toggle button that must be activated by keyboard before the hover tooltip can be displayed

explanation: Under SC 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus, Level AA), the 'Dismissible' requirement specifies that a mechanism is available to dismiss the additional content without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus, typically implemented by pressing Escape.

distractorNotes.a: Dismissible specifically requires a mechanism to dismiss the content without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus.
distractorNotes.c: Automatic timeouts violate the 'Persistent' requirement of SC 1.4.13 unless the content becomes invalid.
distractorNotes.d: A pre-activation toggle button does not fulfill the requirement for dismissing content triggered on hover or focus.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Dismissible requires a way to dismiss hover/focus content without moving pointer or focus.

stem: An evaluator hovers the mouse cursor over a help icon to trigger a popover containing a hyperlink. When the evaluator attempts to move the mouse pointer over the popover to click the link, the popover immediately disappears. What WCAG 2.2 requirement does this violate?

options.text: SC 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts
options.hintText: requires mechanisms to turn off or remap single character shortcuts

options.text: SC 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context)
options.hintText: requires link purpose to be determined from text or programmatic context

options.text: SC 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
options.hintText: requires pointer hover to be movable over additional content without dismissal

options.text: SC 2.5.3 Label in Name
options.hintText: requires accessible names to contain the visible text label of interactive controls

explanation: SC 1.4.13 requires that if pointer hover can trigger the additional content, the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the content disappearing (the 'Hoverable' requirement), allowing users to read or interact with it.

distractorNotes.a: SC 2.1.4 relates to single-character keyboard shortcuts, not mouse hover popovers.
distractorNotes.b: SC 2.4.4 relates to link text clarity, not hover popover persistence.
distractorNotes.d: SC 2.5.3 relates to speech recognition label matching on interactive elements.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Hoverable condition requires that the pointer can move over hover content without it disappearing.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13, a custom tooltip triggered on hover or focus disappears automatically after 4 seconds while the user is still reading it and hovering the trigger. Why does this behavior fail the criterion?

options.text: Tooltips may dismiss automatically after 5 seconds if an audible countdown announcement is provided to screen readers
The persistence requirement applies only to keyboard-focused popovers, while pointer-hover tooltips may use automated timers
Tooltips that contain non-interactive informational text are exempt from the persistence requirement and may fade out
The content must remain visible until the hover trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or it becomes invalid

explanation: The 'Persistent' requirement of SC 1.4.13 mandates that the additional content remains visible until the hover or focus trigger is removed, the user dismisses it, or its information is no longer valid. Automatic timeouts fail this requirement.

distractorNotes.a: SC 1.4.13 does not permit automated dismissal timers, even if audible announcements are provided.
distractorNotes.b: The persistent requirement applies equally to content triggered by pointer hover and keyboard focus.
distractorNotes.c: Informational text tooltips are not exempt; content must remain visible until dismissed, unfocused, or invalid.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.13 Persistent condition mandates hover/focus content remains until trigger is removed or dismissed.

stem: A news website features a live auto-updating breaking news ticker at the top of every page. The ticker starts scrolling automatically upon page load and updates continuously. To satisfy WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide, Level A), what must the author provide?

options.text: A mechanism that pauses ticker scrolling automatically only when the mouse cursor hovers over the ticker
A mechanism allowing users to pause, stop, or hide the moving and auto-updating news feed
An aria-live='polite' region declaration that allows screen readers to announce updates without pausing visual motion
A user preference setting in the account profile that disables ticker animations upon the next page reload

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide), for any moving, blinking, or scrolling information that starts automatically, lasts more than 5 seconds, and is presented in parallel with other content, there must be a mechanism for the user to pause, stop, or hide it.

distractorNotes.a: Hover-only pausing fails to provide a mechanism for keyboard users or touch device users to pause or stop motion.
distractorNotes.c: ARIA live regions assist screen reader users but do not provide a visual pause, stop, or hide mechanism for sighted users.
distractorNotes.d: The pause, stop, or hide mechanism must be immediately available to the user, not deferred to future sessions or profile settings.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.2 requires a mechanism for users to pause, stop, or hide moving or auto-updating content.

stem: An evaluator reviews long-form documentation against WCAG 2.2 Level AAA criteria. Which styling choice directly violates SC 1.4.8 (Visual Presentation) regarding text alignment and line length?

options.text: Text is justified (aligned to both margins) and line length exceeds 80 characters
Text is left-aligned with ragged right edge and line length is 65 characters
Line spacing is set to 1.5 within paragraphs and paragraph spacing is 2 times font size
Foreground and background colors provide a contrast ratio of 7:1

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8 (Visual Presentation, Level AAA) requires that text is not fully justified (aligned to both left and right margins) and line width is no more than 80 characters or glyphs (40 if CJK). Full justification creates uneven spaces ('rivers of white') that impede reading.

distractorNotes.b: Left-aligned text with 65 characters per line conforms to SC 1.4.8 recommendations.
distractorNotes.c: 1.5 line spacing and 2x paragraph spacing are specifically recommended under SC 1.4.8.
distractorNotes.d: 7:1 contrast ratio satisfies Level AAA contrast under SC 1.4.6.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.8 requires non-justified text and line length of 80 characters or fewer (Level AAA).

stem: A web dashboard includes a custom slider widget built with <div> elements to adjust volume. The slider can be dragged with a mouse, but pressing the Left and Right Arrow keys has no effect when the slider is focused. What success criterion does this fail?

options.text: SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast
options.hintText: requires at least 3:1 contrast for user interface components and graphical objects

options.text: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard
options.hintText: requires functionality to be operable through a keyboard interface without specific timings

options.text: SC 3.2.1 On Focus
options.hintText: requires that receiving focus does not initiate an automatic change of context

options.text: SC 1.3.4 Orientation
options.hintText: requires content display not to be restricted to a single orientation unless essential

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard, Level A) requires all functionality of the content to be operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes. Custom sliders must support keyboard adjustment (e.g., arrow keys).

distractorNotes.a: SC 1.4.11 governs visual contrast of graphical objects and components, not operability.
distractorNotes.c: SC 3.2.1 requires that receiving focus does not automatically trigger a context change.
distractorNotes.d: SC 1.3.4 ensures content does not restrict view display to a single orientation.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 mandates all functionality must be operable via a keyboard interface.

stem: When testing an accessible modal dialog, an evaluator observes that tabbing past the last interactive element loops focus back to the first interactive element inside the modal. Does this behavior violate WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap)?

options.text: Yes, because cycling keyboard focus within any DOM element is classified as an automatic keyboard trap under WCAG
Yes, because keyboard navigation must allow focus to escape into the browser address bar at every step of tabbing
No, because SC 2.1.2 applies only to non-HTML embedded plugins (such as PDF viewers or multimedia objects)
No, provided the user can close the dialog and restore page focus using standard keys such as Escape

explanation: Focus trapping within an active modal dialog is standard ARIA practice to prevent tabbing to obscured background content. It does not violate SC 2.1.2 (No Keyboard Trap) as long as the user can escape the dialog using a standard method, such as pressing Escape or activating a Close button.

distractorNotes.a: Confining focus inside a modal is intentional and compliant if standard exit keystrokes (like Escape) work.
distractorNotes.b: Tabbing to background page content while a modal is open is an accessibility defect, not a requirement.
distractorNotes.c: SC 2.1.2 applies to all web content, including HTML and ARIA components; modal focus loops are permitted because Escape provides a standard exit.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.1.2 confirms modal focus loops do not violate the criterion if standard escape exists.

stem: A developer uses CSS flex-direction: row-reverse to display a navigation bar. The visual order of links is 'Home', 'About', 'Contact', but pressing Tab moves focus from 'Contact' to 'About' to 'Home'. Why does this fail WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3 (Focus Order)?

options.text: The focus sequence fails to preserve meaning because DOM order diverges from visual reading order
CSS flex-direction properties are strictly prohibited from being applied to interactive hyperlinks under Level A
All interactive hyperlink elements styled with CSS flexbox must have positive tabindex attribute values declared
Screen readers automatically reorder the virtual reading cursor to match visual CSS layout grids regardless of DOM order

explanation: SC 2.4.3 (Focus Order, Level A) requires that if a web page can be navigated sequentially and the navigation sequences affect meaning or operation, focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning and operability. CSS reordering without DOM adjustment causes confusing focus movement.

distractorNotes.b: CSS flex-direction is not prohibited, but DOM order must match visual order for logical focus navigation.
distractorNotes.c: Using positive tabindex is an anti-pattern that disrupts natural tab flow.
distractorNotes.d: Screen readers linearize content based on DOM order, not visual layout styling like CSS flex-direction.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3 requires focus order to preserve meaning and operability when navigated sequentially.

stem: An evaluator presses the Tab key through an interactive web page. Focus lands on a series of navigation links, but no visible outline, border, background change, or cursor indicator appears. What success criterion is violated?

options.text: SC 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks
options.hintText: requires a mechanism to bypass repeated blocks of content on web pages

options.text: SC 2.4.2 Page Titled
options.hintText: requires web pages to have titles that describe topic or purpose

options.text: SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible
options.hintText: requires keyboard focus indicators to be visually discernible during navigation

options.text: SC 3.1.2 Language of Parts
options.hintText: requires programmatic determination of human language for passage phrases

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.7 (Focus Visible, Level AA) requires that any keyboard operable user interface has a mode of operation where the keyboard focus indicator is visible. Setting outline: none without providing an alternative focus style directly violates this criterion.

distractorNotes.a: SC 2.4.1 requires a mechanism to bypass repeated blocks of content (such as skip links).
distractorNotes.b: SC 2.4.2 requires web pages to have descriptive titles.
distractorNotes.d: SC 3.1.2 requires identifying the human language of parts of text.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.7 requires that any keyboard operable user interface has a visible focus indicator.

stem: When testing a webpage for WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA), a fixed sticky footer covers the bottom 25% of a focused button. Does this fail SC 2.4.11?

options.text: No, because SC 2.4.11 fails only if the focused component is entirely hidden by author content
Yes, because Level AA mandates that 100% of the focused component surface area must remain completely unobscured
Yes, because fixed sticky components are prohibited from overlapping any focusable HTML elements under Level AA
No, provided the sticky footer element has a CSS opacity value set to 0.5 or lower during keyboard navigation

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA) requires that when an item receives keyboard focus, it is not entirely hidden due to author-created content. If it is partially obscured (e.g., 25%), it passes Level AA (though it fails Level AAA SC 2.4.12).

distractorNotes.b: Requiring 100% visibility is the enhanced Level AAA requirement under SC 2.4.12.
distractorNotes.c: Sticky footers are permitted as long as they do not entirely obscure the focused item.
distractorNotes.d: Opacity does not exempt an item if it is completely covered and illegible.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 Level AA requires that the focused component is not entirely hidden by author content.

stem: What is the key difference between WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), Level AA) and SC 2.4.12 (Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced), Level AAA)?

options.text: Level AA applies to native input fields, whereas Level AAA applies exclusively to custom ARIA interactive widgets
Level AA allows partial obscuring if not entirely hidden, whereas Level AAA requires no part to be obscured
Level AA permits obscuring by modal dialogs, whereas Level AAA strictly prohibits all modal dialog window overlays
Level AA evaluates only author-styled focus indicators, whereas Level AAA evaluates default browser focus rings

explanation: Under SC 2.4.11 (Minimum, Level AA), the item cannot be entirely hidden by author content. Under SC 2.4.12 (Enhanced, Level AAA), no part of the focus indicator or focused component may be hidden by author-created content.

distractorNotes.a: Both criteria apply to all user interface components that receive keyboard focus.
distractorNotes.c: Neither criterion prohibits modal dialogs; modals properly manage background focus and visibility.
distractorNotes.d: Both Level AA and Level AAA evaluate whatever focus indicator is active, focusing on degree of obscuring rather than styling origin.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.12 Level AAA requires that no part of the component is hidden by author-created content.

stem: An interactive image gallery on a mobile site allows users to zoom into images using a two-finger pinch gesture. To satisfy WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.1 (Pointer Gestures, Level A), what must the web application provide?

options.text: An option allowing users to shake their mobile device to adjust the image zoom level
A mandatory system voice dictation command that replaces all screen gesture interactions
An alternative single-pointer mechanism, such as plus and minus zoom buttons
A hardware requirement obligating mobile device users to connect an external keyboard

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.1 (Pointer Gestures, Level A) requires that all functionality that uses multipoint or path-based gestures for operation can be operated with a single pointer without a path-based gesture, unless multipoint or path-based gesture is essential. Providing single-pointer zoom buttons satisfies this.

distractorNotes.a: Shaking the device relies on motion actuation (SC 2.5.4) and is not a pointer gesture solution.
distractorNotes.b: Voice dictation is an input modality, not an author-provided single-pointer interface control.
distractorNotes.d: Mobile users cannot be required to attach a physical keyboard to zoom images.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.1 requires single-pointer alternatives for multipoint or path-based gestures.

stem: When auditing a web application, an evaluator presses down the primary mouse button on a 'Delete Account' button. The deletion action triggers immediately on mousedown, before the user releases the button. Why does this violate WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.2 (Pointer Cancellation)?

options.text: Destructive account actions are prohibited from being triggered through mouse pointer clicks under Level A
Pointer cancellation rules apply only to touch screen gestures and do not apply to desktop mouse clicks
Executing destructive actions on mousedown is compliant if a secondary confirmation modal is displayed afterward
The down-event must not trigger the function unless an abort, undo, or up-event mechanism is provided

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.2 (Pointer Cancellation, Level A), for functionality that can be operated using a single pointer, at least one of the following must be true: the down-event is not used to execute the function (it executes on the up-event), an abort/undo mechanism is available, or the down-event is essential. Triggering on mousedown prevents aborting by moving the pointer away.

distractorNotes.a: Destructive actions can be triggered by clicks, provided pointer cancellation rules (like up-event execution) are followed.
distractorNotes.b: SC 2.5.2 applies to all single-pointer interactions, including desktop mouse clicks, touch taps, and stylus inputs.
distractorNotes.c: Triggering functionality on mousedown violates SC 2.5.2 unless down-event execution is essential or up-event/undo is provided.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.2 requires functions to execute on the up-event or provide abort/undo capabilities.

stem: A shopping cart button displays the visible text 'Buy Now' on screen, but its HTML is coded as <button aria-label='Purchase Cart Items'>Buy Now</button>. What barrier does this cause when evaluated with speech recognition software?

options.text: Speech recognition software falls back to targeting the button using its underlying CSS class selector
The shopping cart button fails to render its border correctly in high contrast mode on Windows systems
Screen readers will refuse to speak or present the button in their navigable elements list dialogues
When a user says 'Click Buy Now', the speech software fails to match the accessible name

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3 (Label in Name, Level A), for user interface components with labels that include text or images of text, the accessible name must contain the text that is presented visually. Since aria-label='Purchase Cart Items' completely replaces 'Buy Now' in the accessible name, saying 'Click Buy Now' will not activate the button.

distractorNotes.a: Speech recognition software targets interactive elements via accessible names, not CSS class names.
distractorNotes.b: High contrast mode is unaffected by aria-label naming mismatches.
distractorNotes.c: Screen readers will announce the button using its aria-label ('Purchase Cart Items').

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3 requires visible label text to be included within the programmatic accessible name.

stem: A mobile banking application allows users to clear entered form data by shaking their phone. To conform with WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.4 (Motion Actuation), what two conditions must the application satisfy?

options.text: A conventional UI control must also provide the function, and motion actuation can be turned off
The motion trigger must provide haptic feedback, and sensitivity must be configured via device OS settings
Motion actuation must be restricted to non-essential functions, and device orientation must remain locked
The application must display a visual confirmation prompt each time device motion is detected

explanation: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.4 (Motion Actuation, Level A) requires that functionality triggered by device motion (like shaking or tilting) can also be operated by conventional user interface components (e.g., a 'Clear' button), and the motion response can be disabled to prevent accidental actuation.

distractorNotes.b: Haptic feedback and OS sensitivity settings do not fulfill the requirement for an alternative UI control and disable switch.
distractorNotes.c: SC 2.5.4 does not restrict motion to non-essential functions; it requires conventional controls and a disable mechanism.
distractorNotes.d: Confirmation prompts on every motion trigger do not fulfill the requirement to provide conventional UI alternatives.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.4 requires conventional UI alternatives and the ability to disable motion actuation.

stem: When testing a web application for switch access users (who use single-switch or two-switch scanning software), why do custom interactive components built with <div> elements without tabindex or ARIA roles present severe barriers?

options.text: Switch scanning operates via mouse emulation and bypasses the browser accessibility tree entirely
Switch scanning relies on the accessibility tree and focusable elements to determine scan targets
Switch hardware requires explicit accesskey attributes on every element to register scan targets
Switch software scans only native HTML hyperlink anchors and ignores all form controls

explanation: Switch access systems (such as iOS Switch Control or Android Switch Access) scan through interactive elements exposed via the browser accessibility tree and DOM focus order. Non-semantic <div> elements without tabindex and appropriate roles are skipped during scanning.

distractorNotes.a: Item-mode switch scanning relies on the accessibility tree and DOM focus order to identify scan targets, not mouse emulation.
distractorNotes.c: accesskey attributes are not required for switch scanning; semantic roles and focusability are required.
distractorNotes.d: Switch scanning targets all semantic interactive elements, including buttons, form inputs, and links.

sourceNote: WAI preliminary evaluation notes that switch devices rely on semantic focusable elements to navigate.

stem: An evaluator tests a web application using macOS Voice Control or Dragon NaturallySpeaking. The evaluator says 'Show numbers' to click a custom icon that lacks an accessible name. Why is relying on 'Show numbers' considered a workaround rather than a conformance pass?

options.text: Numbered overlays satisfy SC 4.1.2 because speech software provides a built-in user agent fallback for unlabeled icons
Speech recognition software utilities are strictly prohibited under WCAG 2.2 conformance evaluation methods
Accessible names enable direct voice targeting, whereas missing names force cumbersome numbered overlays
Numbered overlays are preferred because speaking numbers requires fewer syllables than speaking descriptive button labels

explanation: When an interactive control lacks an accessible name, speech users cannot target it directly by speaking its label (e.g., 'Click Search'). They are forced to invoke numbering overlays ('Show numbers') and speak an arbitrary number. This fails SC 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) and hinders efficient interaction.

distractorNotes.a: Assistive technology workarounds (like number overlays) do not excuse author failures to provide accessible names under SC 4.1.2.
distractorNotes.b: Speech recognition software is a key assistive technology evaluated in accessibility audits.
distractorNotes.d: Voice users typically prefer direct speech commands matching visible text; numbered overlays add cognitive load and friction.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 4.1.2 explains that proper accessible names allow direct voice recognition targeting.

stem: According to the Website Accessibility Conformance Evaluation Methodology (WCAG-EM 1.0), what is the first sub-step in Step 1 (Define the Evaluation Scope)?

options.text: Audit all sampled pages using an automated accessibility scanning engine
Interview end users with disabilities to gather subjective usability data
Define the Conformance Target (WCAG version and conformance level)
Select a structured and randomly chosen sample of representative web pages

explanation: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 1 is 'Define the Evaluation Scope'. Sub-step 1.1 is 'Define the Conformance Target', where the evaluator and commissioner specify the target WCAG version (e.g., WCAG 2.2) and conformance level (e.g., Level AA).

distractorNotes.a: Auditing sampled pages occurs in Step 4 of WCAG-EM.
distractorNotes.b: User testing and interviews are supplemental activities outside core WCAG-EM conformance methodology.
distractorNotes.d: Selecting the representative sample occurs in Step 3 of WCAG-EM.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 1.1 defines establishing the target WCAG version and conformance level (A, AA, AAA).

stem: During WCAG-EM Step 1.2 (Define the Scope of the Website), what must an evaluator document if third-party embedded content (such as an external payment portal) cannot be modified by the website owner?

options.text: Document boundaries, URIs, and whether third-party components are included or excluded from evaluation scope
Automatically grant an exemption under WCAG Conformance Requirement 5.2.2 for all embedded external services
Declare the primary website non-conformant immediately without evaluating any pages within author control
Require the third-party vendor to provide a certified Accessibility Conformance Report (VPAT) before starting

explanation: In WCAG-EM Step 1.2, evaluators explicitly define what is in and out of scope, including domain names, subdomains, paths, and third-party content. If third-party items are excluded, this must be transparently documented in the scope statement.

distractorNotes.b: WCAG 5.2.2 does not provide exemptions for partial pages; scope boundaries must be explicitly declared.
distractorNotes.c: Excluding a third-party section from evaluation scope does not invalidate the audit of pages within scope.
distractorNotes.d: While VPATs are useful in procurement, WCAG-EM scoping requires documenting boundaries directly rather than waiting for vendor reports.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 1.2 specifies defining the website scope, including boundaries and third-party content.

stem: In WCAG-EM Step 1.3 (Define the Baseline), what does establishing the 'Accessibility Support Baseline' entail?

options.text: The minimum WCAG success criteria percentage score required for an enterprise product launch
The baseline automated scanning ruleset configured in CI/CD pipelines before manual audits begin
The set of internal organization accessibility coding guidelines applied during sprint planning
Specifying the operating systems, browsers, and assistive technologies against which the site is evaluated

explanation: In WCAG-EM Step 1.3, defining the baseline specifies the combination of user agents (web browsers) and assistive technologies (screen readers, screen magnifiers, speech recognition) supported by the target audience and against which accessibility is evaluated.

distractorNotes.a: WCAG conformance is based on satisfying normative criteria, not a percentage score or threshold.
distractorNotes.b: Automated scanning rulesets are testing tools, not the accessibility support baseline.
distractorNotes.c: Internal coding guidelines are organizational governance documents, not the accessibility support baseline.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 1.3 defines the accessibility support baseline as supported browsers and assistive tech.

stem: In WCAG-EM Step 2 (Explore the Target Website), which activity is specifically performed to ensure that subsequent sample selection is representative?

options.text: Issuing formal conformance compliance certificates for all static pages discovered during exploration
Identifying technologies used, key functionality, distinct page types, and variations in page layout
Running automated scanners across the entire web domain to calculate preliminary compliance scores
Interviewing end users with disabilities to document subjective usability satisfaction ratings

explanation: WCAG-EM Step 2 involves exploring the target website to identify the web technologies used (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PDF), distinct types of web pages (forms, tables, multimedia), key functionalities, and different templates to inform sample selection.

distractorNotes.a: Conformance certificates cannot be issued before the audit is conducted.
distractorNotes.c: Full-domain automated scanning may occur during auditing, but Step 2 focuses on understanding architecture to plan sampling.
distractorNotes.d: User usability testing is outside the core technical methodology of WCAG-EM site exploration.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 2 requires exploring the site to identify technologies, page types, and key functionality.

stem: When constructing the structured sample in WCAG-EM Step 3.1, which criteria guide the selection of representative web pages?

options.text: Selecting only web pages that have logged zero user accessibility complaints during the previous twelve months
Including common pages, diverse functionality, complete processes, and distinct page templates
Selecting pages strictly based on top web analytics traffic volume to maximize user exposure coverage
Selecting exactly one page per top-level navigation menu item regardless of underlying functionality

explanation: WCAG-EM Step 3.1 (Select a Structured Sample) requires including common web pages (homepage, login, search), pages with distinct functions (data tables, forms, multimedia), complete user processes (checkout, registration), and pages using different designs or technologies.

distractorNotes.a: Complaint history is not a technical sampling criterion under WCAG-EM.
distractorNotes.c: While high-traffic pages are important, sampling based solely on traffic misses critical functional workflows and diverse templates.
distractorNotes.d: Menu-based sampling does not ensure coverage of distinct technologies, complete processes, or varied page states.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 3.1 guides selecting structured samples based on diversity, common pages, and complete processes.

stem: Why does WCAG-EM Step 3.2 mandate adding a randomly selected sample of web pages to the structured sample?

options.text: To calculate a statistically valid margin of error for quantitative compliance claims under ISO standards
To guarantee that every single web page across the entire web domain receives identical testing coverage
To validate the structured sample and discover unexpected accessibility issues outside curated templates
To benchmark page load performance and server response times across geographic edge locations

explanation: WCAG-EM Step 3.2 incorporates a randomly selected sample (typically ~10% of the structured sample size) to serve as a validation check. This helps identify edge cases, orphaned pages, or unexpected content authoring practices that were missed during structured selection.

distractorNotes.a: WCAG-EM random sampling is a qualitative validation check to uncover surprises, not an ISO statistical margin calculation.
distractorNotes.b: A random sample of 10% does not provide equal coverage across an entire site.
distractorNotes.d: Performance benchmarking is a DevOps concern unrelated to WCAG-EM sampling methodology.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 3.2 includes randomly selected pages to validate the structured sample and detect surprises.

stem: In WCAG-EM Step 4 (Audit the Selected Sample), what must an auditor record for each sampled web page and success criterion?

options.text: The outcome (pass, fail, or not applicable) along with documentation of any identified failures
The specific code refactoring patches and pull request diffs required to resolve each non-conforming element
A percentage compliance score calculated by dividing passed criteria by total WCAG criteria
The assigned engineering sprint priority and Jira ticket tracking identifiers for bug triage

explanation: WCAG-EM Step 4 requires evaluating each sampled page against all relevant WCAG success criteria and documenting the outcome (e.g., passed, failed, not present/applicable) along with specific failure details, elements, and steps to reproduce.

distractorNotes.b: Code patches and pull requests are engineering remediation deliverables, not the primary record required in WCAG-EM Step 4.
distractorNotes.c: WCAG-EM records outcomes per criterion (pass, fail, N/A), rather than reducing audit results to an arbitrary percentage score.
distractorNotes.d: Jira ticket tracking and sprint assignment are project management tasks that follow reporting, not the WCAG-EM audit outcome record.

sourceNote: WCAG-EM 1.0 Step 4 requires auditing sampled pages and recording outcomes (pass, fail, not applicable).

stem: Which accessibility defect can an automated accessibility scanning tool (such as axe-core or WAVE) reliably detect with high precision without human judgement?

options.text: Whether a video track provides accurate and synchronous captions
Whether an image's alt text accurately describes the instructional context of a diagram
Whether custom navigation links follow a logical reading order for screen reader users
An element that completely lacks an alt attribute in the HTML markup

explanation: Automated rules can reliably verify deterministic syntax and DOM properties, such as a missing alt attribute, duplicate element id values, or missing form <label> associations. Assessing the contextual accuracy of alt text, video captions, or reading order requires human judgement.

distractorNotes.a: Automated tools cannot judge the semantic synchronization and semantic accuracy of captions.
distractorNotes.b: Scanners can check if an alt attribute exists, but cannot judge whether the text accurately describes context.
distractorNotes.c: Logical reading order requires cognitive and context evaluation that automated scanners cannot perform.

sourceNote: W3C Selecting Accessibility Evaluation Tools notes automated tools reliably check syntax like missing alt.

stem: Why do industry accessibility guidelines state that automated testing tools typically detect only 30% to 40% of WCAG success criteria?

options.text: Most criteria require contextual human judgement, such as meaningful alternative text and logical tab flow
Automated scanners cannot evaluate single-page applications that render views dynamically with client-side JavaScript
Automated engines are restricted to evaluating WCAG Level A criteria and cannot evaluate Level AA rules
Browser security models prevent automated test runners from reading computed CSS pseudo-element content

explanation: The majority of WCAG success criteria require human interpretation and context (e.g., whether alt text is meaningful, whether keyboard focus order is logical, whether color is the sole indicator, whether instructions are clear). Automated tools only evaluate rule-based programmatic invariants.

distractorNotes.b: Modern automated tools (like axe-core) run directly within browser runtimes and evaluate dynamic SPA DOM trees.
distractorNotes.c: Automated scanners evaluate both Level A and Level AA criteria where programmatic rules exist (e.g., contrast, labels, roles).
distractorNotes.d: Automated tools have full access to the computed DOM and styles via browser APIs, but cannot replace human evaluation of meaning.

sourceNote: WAI guidance notes automated tools detect ~30-40% of issues because most criteria require human judgement.

stem: An automated scanner flags a text heading as failing SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum). Upon manual inspection, the evaluator finds the text sits over a CSS gradient background, and the actual contrast ratio measured with a color picker across all letters is 6.5:1. How should the evaluator classify this scanner finding?

options.text: A false negative, because the automated tool failed to catch an actual severe visual accessibility violation
An advisory warning, because CSS gradients are classified as non-conforming decorative styles under Level AA
A scanner configuration defect, because automated tools must never be executed on pages with CSS background styling
A false positive, because the scanner flagged compliant text due to complex background gradients

explanation: A false positive occurs when an automated tool flags compliant content as a failure. Many scanners cannot reliably determine the lowest contrast point over CSS gradients or background images and flag an issue even though the content passes upon manual measurement.

distractorNotes.a: A false negative occurs when an actual accessibility failure is missed by the scanner, not when compliant text is flagged.
distractorNotes.b: Gradients are fully permitted in WCAG; the criterion evaluates whether text has sufficient contrast against the gradient.
distractorNotes.c: Automated scanners are routinely run on styled pages, but complex backgrounds require manual verification to confirm contrast.

sourceNote: W3C evaluation tool guidance explains false positives where tools flag compliant complex backgrounds as failures.

stem: When inspecting an interactive custom dropdown component in browser developer tools (such as Chrome or Firefox DevTools), what does the Accessibility Tree pane reveal that the raw DOM Elements tree does not?

options.text: The computed CSS box model dimensions, margins, paddings, and z-index stacking context layers
The active JavaScript event listener bindings and attached keyboard event handler functions
The computed accessible name, role, states, and properties exposed to assistive technologies
The raw HTML source code before browser client-side DOM parsing and script execution

explanation: The browser DevTools Accessibility Tree pane displays the computed accessibility properties of an element—including its computed role, accessible name, description, and ARIA states—as calculated by the browser for assistive technologies.

distractorNotes.a: Box model dimensions and stacking layers are displayed in the Elements and Computed CSS panels, not the Accessibility Tree.
distractorNotes.b: JavaScript event listeners are inspected in the Event Listeners panel in DevTools, not the Accessibility Tree.
distractorNotes.d: Raw HTML source is viewed via Page Source, whereas DevTools inspects the live DOM and computed Accessibility Tree.

sourceNote: W3C AccName 1.2 explains how browsers compute accessible name and role in the accessibility tree.

stem:
An evaluator reviews a search dialog and finds
. When inspecting the accessibility tree in DevTools, what is the expected status of the

options.text: The button remains in the accessibility tree but has its accessible name muted during screen reader reading
The button is removed from the accessibility tree, preventing screen readers from accessing it
The button remains accessible to screen readers while its visual rendering opacity is forced to zero percent
The button is disabled and blocked from receiving native keyboard tab focus during user navigation

explanation: Applying aria-hidden='true' to a container removes the container and all of its DOM descendants from the accessibility tree. As a result, screen readers cannot perceive or interact with the button, even though it remains focusable via the keyboard, creating a severe accessibility barrier.

distractorNotes.a: aria-hidden='true' removes the entire element from the accessibility tree, not just its accessible name.
distractorNotes.c: aria-hidden affects only the accessibility tree, not visual CSS opacity, but it hides content from screen readers.
distractorNotes.d: aria-hidden does not affect keyboard focusability; focusable elements with aria-hidden still receive Tab focus, creating a severe trap/barrier.

sourceNote: WAI-ARIA 1.2 §6.5.3 specifies aria-hidden='true' removes the element and all its children from the accessibility tree.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.1 (Conformance Level), what must a web page satisfy to claim conformance at Level AA?

options.text: Satisfy all Level AA success criteria only, while disregarding all foundational Level A requirements
Satisfy all Level A and AA criteria, with an allowable 5% defect margin for non-critical third-party widgets
Satisfy all Level AA criteria and achieve an overall automated scanner audit score of at least 95%
Satisfy all Level A and all Level AA criteria in full (or provide conforming alternate versions)

explanation: Conformance levels in WCAG are strictly cumulative. To conform at Level AA, the web page must satisfy all Level A success criteria AND all Level AA success criteria in full (or have conforming alternate versions).

distractorNotes.a: Level AA requires satisfying all Level A criteria in addition to Level AA criteria.
distractorNotes.b: WCAG conformance does not permit a margin of error or defect percentage; all applicable criteria must be satisfied in full.
distractorNotes.c: Automated scores cannot establish conformance; Level AA requires meeting all normative Level A and Level AA criteria.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.1 specifies Level AA requires meeting all Level A and AA criteria.

stem: A banking site's multi-step loan application spans four sequential web pages. Pages 1, 2, and 4 conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA, but Page 3 has an inaccessible custom signature component that fails SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard). Can the organization claim Level AA conformance for the loan application?

options.text: Yes, because the majority of pages in the sequential process (75%) successfully pass all Level AA criteria
No, because Conformance Requirement 5.2.3 requires all pages in a complete process to conform
Yes, provided users are given an alternative option to complete the signature by printing a paper document
Yes, because Conformance Requirement 5.2.3 permits claiming partial conformance for multi-step processes if non-conforming steps are disclosed

explanation: Under WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.3 (Complete Processes), when a web page is one of a series of web pages presenting a process (like a transaction or workflow), all web pages in the process must conform at the specified level or better. Conformance cannot be claimed if any step in the process fails.

distractorNotes.a: Conformance cannot be claimed based on passing page percentages within a complete process.
distractorNotes.c: Alternative offline paper workflows do not permit claiming web conformance under 5.2.3.
distractorNotes.d: WCAG 5.2.3 does not permit partial conformance claims for processes; every step in the process must conform.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 Conformance Requirement 5.2.3 mandates that all pages in a complete process must conform.

stem: Under WCAG 2.2, when can a web page rely on a 'Conforming Alternate Version' to satisfy a conformance claim?

options.text: The alternate version conforms, provides equivalent content and function, and has an accessible link
The alternate version is generated dynamically by a third-party accessibility overlay widget upon user request
The alternate version provides simplified plain text while omitting complex data charts and tables
The alternate version provides a text-only summary that can be requested via an email or telephone helpline

explanation: Under the WCAG definition of Conforming Alternate Version, the alternate version must conform at the designated level, provide the same information and functionality in the same human language, be as up to date as the non-conforming version, and be reached via an accessible mechanism from the non-conforming page.

distractorNotes.b: Automated overlay widgets typically fail to provide true conforming alternate versions that meet all Level AA criteria.
distractorNotes.c: Omitting data tables or interactive functionality violates the requirement to provide the same information and functionality.
distractorNotes.d: Offline helplines or email summaries do not meet the definition of a web-based conforming alternate version.

sourceNote: WCAG 2.2 defines Conforming Alternate Version: must conform, provide same content/function, and be accessible.

stem: What is the primary purpose of the W3C Accessibility Conformance Testing (ACT) Rules format in modern web accessibility auditing?

options.text: To replace manual screen reader testing protocols with fully automated headless browser execution pipelines
To define a mandatory European Union regulatory reporting format for public sector web accessibility monitoring
To provide harmonized test rules so different tools and auditors produce consistent results
To administer commercial accreditation and licensing programs for software accessibility audit vendors

explanation: The W3C ACT Rules format defines a standardized way to write accessibility test rules. By harmonizing rule definitions across automated tools, test engines (like axe-core and Alfa), and human testing methodologies, ACT ensures consistent interpretation and testing of WCAG criteria.

distractorNotes.a: ACT Rules do not replace manual testing; they harmonize both automated and manual test rules.
distractorNotes.b: ACT Rules are W3C technical specifications for testing WCAG criteria, not an EU-specific regulatory reporting format.
distractorNotes.d: ACT Rules are open W3C standards, not a commercial accreditation program.

sourceNote: W3C ACT Rules provide harmonized, transparent test procedures to ensure consistent evaluation across tools.
